items.title: Responses of large language model-based chatbots to simulated psychotic ideation across repeated interactions
items.abstract: Following the development of widely accessible large language model-based chatbot systems, concerns have emerged that such systems may reinforce psychotic ideation through affirmation of delusional content. However, systematic evaluations of chatbot responses to psychotic scenarios remain limited. We hypothesized that chatbot responses would become increasingly affirmatory over repeated interactions with the user. To test this, we evaluated the responses of ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Replika to simulated psychosis scenarios. Conversations were conducted across seven consecutive days in two languages. Responses were coded for chatbot stance toward psychotic content, recommendation to seek clinical assessment, presence of follow-up questions, and additional advice. Mixed-effects and linear regression models were used, including cluster-robust linear probability models for binary outcomes. As simulated symptom severity increased across days, ChatGPT responses became less affirmatory, DeepSeek responses remained relatively stable, and Replika responses became more affirmatory; latter two trajectories differed significantly from ChatGPT. Response variability decreased for ChatGPT and Replika but increased for DeepSeek across days. The effects of language and symptom domain were non-significant. Recommendation rates differed significantly between systems. DeepSeek and Replika provided potentially harmful advice, including discontinuation of antipsychotic treatment, in 21% and 37% of conversations, respectively. These findings suggest that affirmation of psychotic ideation significantly varies across different chatbots and does not appear to be an unavoidable consequence of large language model deployment. Furthermore, they underscore the need for developing explicit safety standards governing chatbot responses to psychotic content.

items.title: REST: Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics Supervision for Gene Expression Prediction from Histopathological HE-Stained Images
items.abstract: Histopathology is central to cancer diagnosis, but morphology in Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-stained images does not directly reveal the molecular states that characterize disease heterogeneity and inform tumor characterization, prognostic assessment, and biomarker discovery. Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) measures spatially resolved gene expression, providing molecular information within tissue architecture, yet differences in assay coverage and spot informativeness make paired HE--ST observations unequally reliable for representation learning. We propose Reliability-Guided Spatial Transcriptomics (REST) supervision with Biological Program Bank (BPB), a program-structured and reliability-guided ST-supervised training framework for predicting molecular information from H\&E images. REST constructs BPB from curated signature, pathway, and cell-type gene sets to provide a shared structure for ST encoding, reliability estimation, and molecular reconstruction. Guided by BPB, Spot-Reliability Contrastive Alignment (SRCA) measures the reliability of each spot from assay-level program coverage and spot-level activity dispersion, and reweights HE--ST alignment accordingly. Biology-Informed Program Reconstruction (BIPR) further uses learnable program queries to reconstruct member-gene expression from histological morphology. REST's training corpus comprised 209 samples (407,475 spots across 16 organs); evaluation used 70 disjoint samples (230,056 spots across eight organs) for gene-expression, pathway-activity, and cell-signature prediction. REST achieved the highest Macro correlation among state-of-the-art ST-supervised training methods and outperformed existing pathology foundation models. Code is available at https://github.com/lanfz2000/REST.

items.abstract: Lasswell's five-question formula remains a durable frame for analyzing source, message, channel, audience and effect. items.title: Rethinking LLM Fine-Tuning via Weight Space Reparameterization: Preserving Safety during Downstream Adaptation
items.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on downstream tasks often weakens their previously aligned safety behavior, creating an inherent trade-off between task adaptation and safety preservation. Existing approaches attempt to mitigate this issue by identifying safety-relevant neurons, layers, or update directions in the original parameter space. However, safety-related information is often distributed across many directions in this space, causing downstream updates to overwrite parameters that encode safety behavior. We propose WSR-Tune, a Weight Space Reparameterization-based fine-tuning framework that preserves safety during downstream adaptation. Our approach constructs a safety-conditioned basis and reparameterizes the weight matrices such that safety-relevant information becomes concentrated in a small subset of directions. We then identify safety-critical directions and freeze them in the reparameterized space, while updating the remaining complementary directions for downstream adaptation. By explicitly structuring the parameter space to disentangle safety and task information, our method reduces interference between objectives and enables simultaneous preservation of safety and improvement in downstream performance. Experimental results show that our method achieves a more favorable trade-off between downstream performance and safety retention, demonstrating its effectiveness for reliable LLM fine-tuning.

items.title: Reviving Professorware: An Agentic Approach
items.abstract: Maintaining legacy bioinformatics software remains a longstanding challenge in research computing. Many tools are developed by PhD students and remain in active use long after their graduation, even when the underlying technology stack has become outdated or unsupportable. Yet full rewrites demand substantial developer time, which research group leaders are seldom able to allocate and new recruits are rarely motivated to undertake. Large language model (LLM)-based coding assistants offer a potential new approach to this problem, but their effectiveness in real-world research software engineering (RSE) contexts remains poorly characterized.We present a case study in AI-assisted legacy modernisation using KEGGanim, a Perl CGI web application that overlays time-series gene expression data onto KEGG pathway diagrams as animated visualisations. The tool, originally developed by the BIIT group, was first published in 2008 and has remained available since then. It is currently maintained by the ELIXIR Estonia Node at the University of Tartu as one of ELIXIR Estonia’s Node Services. The tool was rewritten from scratch using Claude Code (Anthropic) as the primary development tool. The new implementation uses FastAPI, React 18, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose, replacing static GIF output with interactive SVG animations while preserving full data pipeline logic including KEGG gene mapping, ENSG identifier conversion, and KNN imputation.The rewrite was conducted as an instrumented RSE experiment. Development sessions were logged manually for time attribution; all LLM conversation logs were preserved in JSONL format for post-hoc extraction of human intervention counts, token usage, and effort distribution across project phases. Functional correctness was validated using a four-level regression suite against reference fixtures captured from the legacy production instance.We report on the feasibility, efficiency, and failure modes of LLM-driven legacy modernisation, and discuss implications for sustainable tool development within ELIXIR and the wider RSE community.

items.title: Rewriting the Care Algorithm: Clinical Practice in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) has grown significantly since its introduction and inception in the late 1950s and has become interwoven into healthcare. Objective: This narrative review evaluates practice concerns and perceptions associated with the heightened demand for AI in healthcare, particularly as a cost-saving tool for nursing and providers. Methods: Online databases included PubMed and CINAHL. Boolean terminology included healthcare and AI, AI and nursing, as well as AI and ethics. Results were limited to complete online articles written within the previous five years. Initial searches yielded over 55,469 results. Results: Despite a growing push from federal agencies and hospital systems to incorporate their use, there is no definitive consensus on the application of AI in healthcare. This may cause harm to patients as AI tools are not consistently accurate, may misdiagnose, and have potential for "unconscious" bias. However, significant time and cost may be saved with care algorithm implementation. Conclusions: Careful evaluation and ethical analysis are warranted on a case-by-case basis prior to commencement. Nursing staff and healthcare providers are integral to the "care algorithm" and cannot be removed from direct patient care without potential harm.

items.title: Risk-Driven Ergonomic Redesign of a Woodworking CNC Workstation: WERA Analysis, Anthropometric Translation, and a Hydraulic Lift Table Proposal
items.abstract: Background: Wood-based manufacturing still relies on repetitive manual material handling around CNC workstations, exposing workers to awkward postures, high physical demands, and prolonged standing. At the observed workstation, the primary ergonomic problems were associated with loading, unloading, inspection, and palletizing activities rather than with the machining cycle itself. Objective: This study aimed to address ergonomic issues associated with CNC workstation activities by proposing an ergonomic intervention involving the redesign of a CNC support workstation with a hydraulic lift table. The contribution of this study lies in integrating task-level ergonomic risk assessment with anthropometric design to develop a practical engineering proposal for wood manufacturing. Methods: A quantitative descriptive approach was employed, incorporating direct observation, postural documentation, interviews, Nordic Body Map screening, anthropometric measurements, and the Workplace Ergonomic Risk Assessment (WERA) method. The study involved 14 workers, comprising 5 CNC operators and 9 helpers. Results: The WERA scores were 28 for operators and 41 for helpers, indicating greater ergonomic risk exposure among helpers. The predominant risk factors were shoulder posture, neck posture, forceful exertion, repetition, and task duration. Anthropometric analysis informed the proposed design of a hydraulic lift table with a platform measuring 1,300 × 1,100 mm, an adjustable height range of 300–900 mm, and a minimum lifting capacity of 100 kg. Conclusion: Helper tasks represent the most critical source of ergonomic risk at the CNC workstation. The proposed hydraulic lift table offers a feasible engineering intervention to reduce ergonomic risks and support occupational health and safety in wood manufacturing.

items.title: RL-Robotutor: a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for multimodal robot tutoring
items.abstract: Personalised robot tutoring requires real-time pedagogical decision-making under uncertain and multimodal learner states. Existing intelligent tutoring and robot-assisted learning systems often rely on static rules, single-modality learner modelling, or short-term correctness-oriented optimisation, which limits their capacity to balance knowledge acquisition, engagement, retention, and safe embodied interaction. RL-Robotutor is presented as a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that integrates cognitive knowledge-tracing signals, facial-expression and gaze-derived affective cues, and behavioural interaction logs through transformer-based fusion. A PPO-trained meta-policy selects among specialised modules for learner assessment, curriculum adaptation, strategy selection, and reflective feedback, while a hybrid reward combines immediate learning performance, engagement, long-term learning gain, and safety. The evidence is reported by source: five public knowledge-tracing datasets assess the cognitive prediction component; controlled simulator experiments assess policy learning, reward ablation, and multimodal fusion; and a randomised robot-tutoring study assesses embodied interaction with 120 undergraduate participants. RL-Robotutor outperforms rule-based, flat reinforcement-learning, knowledge-tracing, and LLM-based comparators. In the human study, the learning gain is 0.62, compared with 0.40 for the rule-based robot condition. The full hybrid reward improves simulator learning gain by 19% over correctness-only optimisation, and full multimodal fusion improves simulator engagement by 17% over text-only modelling. Jetson Orin deployment achieves 48 ms inference latency with an absolute AUC reduction of 0.007, supporting real-time edge execution.

items.title: ROLE OF GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CONTENT MARKETING: IMPACT ON CONSUMER PERCEPTION AND BRAND INTERACTION
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed content marketing by enabling the creation of personalized, scalable, and data-driven marketing content.This study aims to examine the role of generative AI in content marketing and its impact on consumer perception and brand interaction.The research adopts a descriptive and analytical design, using primary data collected from 120 respondents who actively engage with digital platforms.A structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale was employed to measure key constructs, including generative AI content quality, consumer perception, perceived authenticity, trust, and brand interaction.The collected data were analysed using SPSS, applying statistical techniques such as reliability analysis, factor analysis, correlation, and regression.The findings reveal that generative AI-driven content has a significant positive impact on consumer perception and brand interaction.The study also highlights that perceived authenticity plays a crucial role in building consumer trust, which in turn strongly influences brand interaction.Furthermore, consumer perception and trust partially mediate the relationship between AI-generated content and brand interaction.While generative AI enhances marketing efficiency and engagement, concerns related to authenticity and trust remain important considerations.The study contributes to the existing literature by providing empirical evidence on the effectiveness of generative AI in content marketing and offers practical insights for marketers to develop balanced strategies that integrate technological capabilities with human creativity.The findings are particularly relevant for organizations seeking to enhance consumer engagement and build sustainable brand relationships in the evolving digital marketing landscape.

items.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
items.abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $Ψ_0$, $ω$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.

items.title: RouterWorld: Scaling Conversational AI with Latency-Aware LLM Routing
items.abstract: Conversational AI systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) require routing mechanisms that balance answer quality and response latency at scale. However, existing LLM routing benchmarks assume full observability of all candidate model outcomes, under-emphasize latency as a first-class metric, and fragment evaluation across heterogeneous protocols misaligned with real-world settings. We introduce RouterWorld, a comprehensive benchmark for LLM routing in conversational GenAI. RouterWorld unifies 371k single-turn responses and 76k multi-turn agentic trajectories, adopts natural user interactions with a standardized LLM-as-a-judge protocol, and decouples efficiency from transient pricing via hardware-grounded latency annotations. Crucially, RouterWorld formalizes routing under partial observability through two setups: Cold-Start, which restricts learning to sparse, static logs, and Voyager, which models continuous data streams where routing decisions shape future training distributions. Evaluating 13 routing baselines, we find that most routers over-emphasize accuracy while ignoring latency under partial observability. Code and benchmark data are publicly available.

items.title: Routing Leaves a Trace: Zero-Logit Architectural Segregation of Frontier Mixture-of-Experts vs. Dense Language Models
items.abstract: As frontier large language models transition from monolithic dense networks to sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, determining architectural provenance in black-box text has become a critical forensic challenge. Existing detectors operate under binary paradigms (human vs. machine) or require token-level probability logits that are suppressed by commercial API gateways. In this short paper, we present an empirical investigation into whether sparse expert routing leaves an indelible post-hoc syntactic signature in generated prose. Evaluating across N=120 verified long-form corporate documents (>=750 words, mean 1,050.0 words) spanning three frontier MoE architectures (DeepSeek-V3 671B, Nemotron-3 Super 120B, MiniMax-01 456B) and three frontier Dense architectures (Qwen-2.5 72B, Llama-3.3 70B, Cohere Command-R+ 104B), we evaluate discrimination across clausal subordination entropy (H_clause) and macro-discursive coherence decay (Delta_decay). Our empirical results demonstrate: (1) Binary MoE vs. Dense architectural segregation achieves an AUROC of 0.9897 (94.13% accuracy) on unperturbed text, remaining stable at 0.9424 AUROC (84.40% accuracy) under aggressive 11B DIPPER neural paraphrasing (L=60, O=60). (2) Within isolated cohorts, fine-grained model attribution achieves 90.00% Top-1 accuracy across MoE architectures (DeepSeek vs. Nemotron vs. MiniMax; Top-2 Recall: 100.0%) and 80.00% Top-1 accuracy across Dense architectures (Qwen vs. Llama vs. Cohere; Top-2 Recall: 100.0%). (3) In global 6-way attribution (n=60), the framework achieves 73.33% Top-1 accuracy (Mean Reciprocal Rank 0.8306 vs. 0.1667 random chance; permutation p = 0.0010), maintaining 68.33% Top-1 accuracy under strict Leave-One-Topic-Out out-of-domain cross-validation. These findings confirm that sparse mixture routing imprints distinct clausal branching dynamics that survive vocabulary substitution.

items.title: Safety Incidents Among Workers in Oil and Gas Downstream Companies in Port Harcourt Metropolis, Nigeria
items.abstract: The study investigated the appraisal of safety incidents among workers in selected oil and gas downstream companies in Port Harcourt metropolis. The study design was a descriptive survey design and study population consisted of 1500 workers oil and gas downstream companies in Port Harcourt. A non-stratified sampling method was used in selecting the sample of the study which consisted of 340 workers. A self- structured questionnaire was the instrument of the study. The study found that 56% of the respondents were 25-30 years old, 28% were 31 – 35 years old, 14% were 36 – 40 years old while 2% were 41 years old above, 78% of the respondents were males while 22% were females. The study further revealed that the types of safety incidents that were common among workers in oil and gas downstream companies in Port Harcourt metropolis includes truck tanker accident in transit, Truck tanker accident within the terminal or station etc and that the injuries that are common in oil and gas downstream companies in Port Harcourt metropolis includes back injury (ergonomic), sprain of a limb etc. The study concluded that workers at different levels in the Port Harcourt metropolis oil and gas downstream sector experienced safety incidents. Therefore, the study recommended that companies particularly, petroleum products retailers should commit to developing sound HSE culture among workers by way of robust HSE policies and personnel training programs. These programs would address both unsafe practices and unsafe situations.

items.title: Safety Intelligence in Aviation: Thinking Outside the box
items.abstract: Recent fatal accidents in aviation have once again highlighted the critical importance of safety and the need for continuous advancement in safety management approaches. Over the years, the accumulation of vast amounts of safety data and information has not only enhanced our understanding of operational risks but has also introduced new challenges related to data complexity, interpretation, and effective utilization. The increasing complexity of aviation operations, coupled with the rapid growth of data-driven technologies, has further challenged traditional safety management approaches that are predominantly reactive and compliance-based.In this context, the concept of safety intelligence has emerged as a promising paradigm that transforms raw operational data into actionable insights for proactive and predictive safety decision-making. This review article synthesizes existing literature on safety intelligence, safety management systems, human factors, and data analytics to provide a comprehensive conceptual understanding of safety intelligence in aviation. Particular attention is given to the integration of data-driven approaches with human interpretation, organizational learning, and safety culture.The ultimate goal of this line of research has become increasingly evident in light of recent aviation accidents, emphasizing the need for a deeper and more holistic understanding of safety intelligence to enhance global flight safety.

items.title: Safety Mid-Training: Internalizing LLM Safety as a Foundational Capability
items.abstract: Safety alignment for large language models (LLMs) is primarily performed during post-training, while recent work has also begun incorporating safety data into pre-training. Yet safety can degrade when later training no longer includes safety data, and gains in safety often come at the cost of general capability. This tension suggests that safety and general reasoning should not be treated as separate training goals. We instead view safety as an LLM capability that can be learned through a reasoning structure shared with general tasks. Both require the model to understand intent or task goals, apply relevant knowledge, and reason about potential consequences. We introduce safety mid-training, a stage between pre-training and post-training that jointly develops safety and general reasoning through this shared structure. Given safety and utility prompts, the base model generates structured documents and reasoning traces that are then used for mid-training. Safety mid-training reduces average attack success rate (ASR) by 72% to 81% relative to Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B base models, while also improving general capability. The benefits persist through subsequent post-training. After general-only SFT, mid-trained models largely retain their safety, achieving lower ASR than the baselines without sacrificing general capability. They also retain safety under general-only GRPO without safety rewards, while subsequent RL reaches a better safety-utility frontier when initialized from the mid-trained models. Together, these results suggest that learning safety and general reasoning within a shared mid-training stage can reduce the safety-utility trade-off and make safety more robust to subsequent training.

items.title: Safety Offset Learning: When Benign Fine-Tuning Misaligns LLMs
items.abstract: Safety risks from fine-tuning are commonly characterized by the harmfulness of the training data:harmful fine-tuning is considered dangerous, while benign fine-tuning is often assumed to preservealignment. We argue that this view misses a more fundamental factor-the behavioral transition inducedby supervision. Harmful fine-tuning and safety-degrading benign fine-tuning can both be understoodas learning the same refusal-to-compliance transition, but on different data distributions. We studywhether such a transition learned on benign inputs can generalize to harmful requests. We constructbenign examples that an aligned model initially tends to refuse and pair them with their originalharmless responses, creating a discrepancy between the model's initial refusal and the supervisedanswer. Fine-tuning on these examples increases harmful compliance, but only when two conditionshold together: the discrepancy is large enough, and it cannot be resolved through a narrow surface-levelshortcut. With the induced discrepancy matched, varying only whether it is localized changes harmfulcompliance by an order of magnitude; raising the discrepancy does not help while a shortcut remainsavailable, and removing the shortcut does not help while the discrepancy is small. Building on thisobservation, we introduce SAFEOFF, a dataset of benign instructions rewritten to raise the alignedmodel's refusal likelihood and paired with their original answers. Across three aligned LLMs and threesafety benchmarks, SAFEOFF substantially weakens safety alignment despite containing no explicitharmful supervision, suggesting that fine-tuning safety depends not only on what data a model sees, butalso on which behavioral boundary the supervision moves.

items.title: Same Child, Different Home: How Large Language Models Forecast the Futures of Identical Twins Raised Apart
items.abstract: Public agencies have begun to consider AI tools for judgments about children. In Japan, the Children and Families Agency developed an AI tool to support child-abuse assessments at child guidance centres and decided in 2025 not to introduce it after tests showed low accuracy. Before such tools are used, it matters what an AI weighs when it forecasts a child's future. This study does not measure how real children develop. It measures how large language models (LLMs) forecast the future of a child when only the child's household differs. We use the logic of the classic "twins reared apart" design: we create fictional identical twin pairs with exactly the same child profile at birth, place one twin in a reference household and the other in a household that differs in specified conditions, and ask LLMs to forecast each child's outcomes at ages 15, 18 and 30. Because the child profile is identical within each pair, any difference in forecasts is attributable to the household conditions given to the model. All children and households are fictional; no data on real children are used.

items.title: Scalable and robust deep learning models for space debris detection across orbital regimes and observation platforms
items.abstract: Space debris poses a significant threat to space missions, requiring accurate and real-time detection across multiple orbital regimes and observation platforms. This study aims to develop a scalable YOLOv12-PSO framework for accurate space debris detection and to investigate its effectiveness in improving real-time performance, robustness, and detection accuracy across orbital environments. A publicly available space debris image dataset containing synthetic and real images was used to train and evaluate the proposed framework under varying orbital conditions. The proposed system integrates YOLOv12 with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) for hyperparameter tuning, while preprocessing steps such as resizing, normalization, and data augmentation are applied to improve robustness. The model is trained and tested on the dataset for object detection, optimization, and performance assessment. Experimental results demonstrate that the optimized model outperforms baseline approaches, achieving Precision (0.89), Recall (0.87), F1-Score (0.88), and mAP (0.78). Comparative evaluation against Baseline YOLOV12, YOLOV12v8m, YOLOV12v8s, YOLOV12v5s, GEO-SPANN, and CNN-based methods confirms improved detection accuracy and real-time inference performance under noisy and complex conditions. This work presents a novel scalable deep learning framework integrating YOLOv12 with Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), enhancing detection accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, while contributing to advanced space situational awareness systems, autonomous space debris monitoring, and improved orbital debris mitigation and management strategies. The proposed YOLOv12-PSO framework supports autonomous space debris monitoring and provides a policy-relevant tool for space traffic management, contributing to improved orbital safety, collision risk reduction, and long-term sustainability of space mission operations and satellite environment governance.

items.title: Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs
items.abstract: Building capable language models for India requires scalable multilingual data and robust evaluation. We introduce Nemotron-Pretraining-Indic-v1, a synthetic pretraining corpus of approximately 2.83 trillion tokens covering all 22 scheduled Indian languages in native script and twelve in romanized form. It is the largest openly released Indic pretraining corpus. Using our GPU-accelerated pipeline, we translate curated English documents, assess translation quality, and repair low-quality outputs while preserving technical content and document structure and maintaining source traceability. Through continued-pretraining experiments across twelve languages, we show that combining our synthetic corpus with natural Indic text improves knowledge and reasoning over a public-corpus baseline. Additional experiments show how data volume, script coverage, and Indic training share affect English performance. We also introduce the Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, a multilingual benchmark suite for evaluating Indic language models across chat, instruction following, reasoning, knowledge, code, and translation. The suite combines existing Indic benchmarks with task-aware translations of English benchmarks, using automated quality assessment, targeted correction, and native-speaker review in a human-in-the-loop pipeline. We use the suite to comprehensively benchmark contemporary open-weight Indic and multilingual models across capabilities and languages, revealing substantial variation across tasks and languages. Together, these resources provide a scalable foundation for developing and evaluating more capable Indic language models.

items.title: Scientific Agentic Engineering: A Framework for Reliable AI Agents in Research Software
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping how research software is developed. Tools and patterns ranging from “vibe coding” through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and autonomous agents now offer compelling productivity gains, but their adoption in scientific computing surfaces failure modes that general-purpose evaluation does not catch: silent unit conversions, violated conservation laws, hallucinated physics, loss of numerical precision, and quietly broken reproducibility. These failures share a signature: nothing visible goes wrong. The AI ecosystem itself is moving fast, leaving RSEs to make consequential integration decisions with little shared vocabulary or principled guidance. This talk introduces Scientific Agentic Engineering, the central contribution of an in-progress 2026 Better Scientific Software (BSSw) Fellowship: a tool-agnostic methodology for integrating AI agents into high-stakes scientific software workflows. The framework defines how agents, scientific skills, and MCP servers should be structured around validation loops, explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and domain-specific safeguards. Every task moves through a short workflow (frame, plan and critique, implement, verify), with decisions recorded throughout, and the framework maps each documented failure mode to the stage where it is cheapest to catch. The intent is not to recommend any particular AI tool but to articulate foundational concepts that remain valid as the underlying technology changes. I will share three artifacts from the fellowship: The Framework (published July 2026). Shared vocabulary, its principles and workflow, structural guidance on where safeguards live, and a pattern catalog of named practices, each tied to the failure it counters. The Reference Workflow. A structured exercise in which RSEs use AI tools to build a small weather-model error-statistics application, applying the framework to avoid the failure modes it documents. The Community Repository. A curated starter set of scientific MCP server templates, agent skills such as unit checkers and conservation-law validators, and agent configuration examples, designed to be starting points for the community to adapt to a variety of scientific domains. These artifacts are by design community resources, and broader adoption is the explicit aim of the remaining milestones, which include an interactive online tutorial series comparing purpose-built scientific agents with general-purpose tools, a recorded live workshop published for asynchronous access, and a BSSw.io blog post directing the community to the project’s resources. This work engages the conference theme directly by advancing AI-assisted scientific software development from ad-hoc experimentation toward a disciplined, transferable engineering practice.

items.title: SDS screen-positive prediction from structured questionnaires in university students: a comparative evaluation of large language model prompting strategies
items.abstract: Introduction Large language models (LLMs) can render structured questionnaire variables as natural-language profiles, but their value in mental-health screening cannot be judged from a single fixed-threshold score. We evaluated LLM prompt conditions in a cross-questionnaire benchmark for predicting screen-positive status on the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) among undergraduates. The intended application was an offline methodological benchmark using previously collected questionnaire data, not a shorter alternative to direct SDS administration. Methods De-identified records were assigned to Development (n=1,951), Test (n=2,186), and Holdout (n=2,258) grade cohorts. We evaluated logistic regression, XGBoost, and 12 model-prompt conditions at the fixed 0.5 threshold and at thresholds selected only in Development-validation. We also examined paired bootstrap differences, ranking stability, scale correlations, grouped ablations, cohort shift, calibration intercepts and slopes, alternative expected calibration error specifications, representative repeated calls at temperatures 0 and 0.1, sex-stratified performance, and per-1,000 screening scenarios. Results At the fixed 0.5 threshold on Test, GPT E1, Gemini E2, and XGBoost achieved macro-F1 values of 0.732, 0.730, and 0.674. At Development-derived thresholds of 0.38, 0.50, and 0.174, the corresponding macro-F1 values were 0.702, 0.730, and 0.660. At the Development-selected specificity target, XGBoost achieved a Test macro-F1 of 0.738. Pairwise intervals showed no clear fixed-0.5 macro-F1 difference among the three highest-ranked LLM conditions. XGBoost yielded the lowest Brier scores. The combined-sample Spearman correlation between SDS and SAS was 0.60. Together with the ablation results, this correlation indicated predictive information distributed across overlapping questionnaire groups rather than dependence on a single measured group. In repeated calls across the complete Holdout cohort, inconsistent-case rates were 23.6% for GPT E1 and 1.5% for Gemini E2. Temperature 0 did not clearly eliminate GPT E1 instability in the representative 400-case subset. Discussion Model conclusions depended on both the threshold and the metric. Certain LLM prompt conditions were competitive at specific operating points, but the evidence did not establish a stable or general advantage over structured-data models. Nor did it establish external validity, clinical diagnostic utility, or reduced questionnaire burden. Threshold choice, calibration, output validity, and repeated-call stability therefore require separate evaluation before prospective use.

items.title: SECURITY AND PRIVACY CHALLENGES IN AGENTIC AI SYSTEMS
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems can plan multi-step tasks, use external tools, retrieve information, andtake actions with limited human intervention. These capabilities create security and privacy risks beyond those found inconventional question-answering systems. An agent may encounter malicious instructions in retrieved content, misuse anauthorized tool, expose confidential context, retain unnecessary personal data, or continue a harmful action through a chain ofotherwise ordinary steps. This paper presents a risk-aware framework for analysing these challenges across the agent lifecycle. Itorganizes the main risks into instruction and prompt injection, excessive agency, insecure tool integration, data leakage, identityand access-control weaknesses, memory risks, and insufficient monitoring. The proposed approach combines least-privilegepermissions, separation of trusted instructions from untrusted data, explicit approval for high-impact actions, privacy-awarememory, output validation, and audit logging. A staged evaluation plan is described using threat scenarios and measurablesecurity and privacy indicators. This paper is a design-oriented study and does not claim experimental results or a deployedsecurity product. Its central argument is that agentic AI should be treated as a socio-technical system whose safety depends on themodel, tools, data, permissions, and surrounding operational controls

items.title: Selecting the Best Few with Human Evaluators: Adaptively Combining Ratings and Pairwise Comparisons
items.abstract: This paper considers a decision-maker tasked with identifying the $k$ best items from a large pool of candidates, such as job applicants, LLMs, award nominees, or new product ideas. The decision-maker learns about the items' quality by soliciting human evaluations. Each evaluation can be costly, so the decision-maker aims to use the limited evaluation budget efficiently by allocating evaluations adaptively. A key consideration is the form of evaluation to solicit, which should be something evaluators are comfortable providing. Two popular forms are ratings and pairwise comparisons, and we allow for both, as they may be especially useful in combination given the limited budget. Ratings can be used early on to get a coarse picture of which items are good and which are not. As that picture forms, comparisons can refine the ordering of the good items, narrowing in on the ultimate top-$k$ selection. To solve the allocation problem, we develop an adaptive algorithm built from two allocation policies. The first, our primary contribution, is based on a surrogate objective that is naturally forward-looking, valuing evaluations that help inform what to evaluate in future rounds, not just those that directly improve the selection decision. The decision rule is interpretable, and we prove that it is asymptotically consistent. Late in the evaluation process, when being forward-looking is less productive, we construct a myopic policy and a criterion for switching to it. In simulation, the method gives insight into how to combine these two types of evaluations, and beats the (limited) existing benchmarks.

items.title: SENSE: A Sensor-Centric Multimodal Evidence Chain for Teaching Evaluation in Smart Classrooms
items.abstract: Smart-classroom teaching evaluation increasingly relies on heterogeneous sensing sources, including classroom cameras, microphones, speech-recognition systems, and learning-platform interaction logs. Existing systems often treat these streams as separate analytical inputs, with insufficient attention to cross-modal alignment, missing-sensor robustness, and evidence-grounded large-language-model reasoning. This paper proposes SENSE (Sensor-Evidence Network for Smart-Classroom Evaluation), a sensor-centric framework that organizes classroom evaluation as an end-to-end evidence chain. Visual behavior, acoustic-semantic content, and learning-platform events are aligned in lesson-level time windows and converted into structured evidence packets. Available learning-outcome anchors provide contextual evidence to the semantic evaluator, whereas expert ratings are retained exclusively as external validation references. A DeepSeek-based semantic evaluator then generates engagement, instructional-content, interaction-quality, and teaching-feedback judgments under a fixed output schema. The framework was evaluated using 48 college-English lessons, 48 videos, 48 audio recordings, 4628 timestamped learning-platform interaction logs, and 960 valid student-window observation instances. Compared with a transparent rule-based operational baseline, SENSE reduced the engagement-evaluation error from 12.3% to 5.8%, reduced the content-coverage error from 14.5% to 6.2%, and increased the correlation with the mean expert score from 0.71 to 0.89. Under 30% random evidence removal, the correlation remained 0.80. The results indicate that teaching evaluation benefits from a multimodal sensor-evidence and semantic-reasoning process rather than a single behavior-recognition task.

items.abstract: To analyze factors related to the meaning attributed to police work and understand elements associated with strengthening or weakening the perception of purpose in the role. Method: An integrative literature review was conducted through searches in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, SciELO, and the Virtual Health Library, considering studies published from January 2021 to September 2026 in Portuguese, English, and Spanish. Original studies addressing police officers’ professional experiences were included, considering occupational identity, job satisfaction, work engagement, motivation, organizational support, stress, occupational strain, and work-life balance. Study selection was presented using a flowchart based on PRISMA 2020, resulting in 19 included studies. Results: Findings showed that the meaning of work is influenced by individual, relational, and institutional factors. Professional identity, recognition, organizational support, organizational justice, autonomy, satisfaction, and resilience were associated with more positive work experiences, whereas workload, stress, emotional demands, work-family conflicts, and organizational difficulties were associated with occupational strain and weakening of the bond with the activity. Conclusion: Loss of purpose should not be understood solely as a lack of individual motivation, but as a phenomenon related to the concrete conditions under which police work is performed. Strengthening institutional support, professional recognition, work schedule organization, and occupational health care may contribute to maintaining the meaning attributed to police work and sustaining healthier and more meaningful professional relationships throughout the career. Such measures may reduce the distance between professional expectations and everyday work experiences in diverse institutional contexts and at different stages of professional trajectories over time.

items.title: SFOE Geothermal Workshop 2026
items.abstract: Geothermal Energy: Aligning Research with Project Needs The development of geothermal energy in Switzerland relies not only on the implementation of new technologies but also on a better understanding of the subsurface and its various potential uses. A key challenge is to better bridge the gap between research advances and the practical needs of projects. With this in mind, the second edition of the geothermal workshop organized by the SFOE in September brought together nearly 80 participants from the research community, industry, and public authorities. The event highlighted research efforts, field experiences, and challenges related to project development, focusing on three themes: subsurface exploration, underground heat storage, and next-generation geothermal systems. The first part of the day was devoted to geothermal exploration and developments since the first edition of the workshop in 2024, which was entirely dedicated to this topic. swisstopo provided a detailed overview of the entire process for managing geothermal data from exploration projects supported by the federal government, from collection through quality control (QC) to publication. The resulting lessons learned and future prospects were also discussed. A roundtable bringing together representatives from research, industry, and swisstopo then provided an opportunity to discuss the progress made in transferring research results into practice, as well as the obstacles still encountered—whether technical in nature or related to the adoption of these innovations and their integration into the exploration programs of commercial projects. The discussions showed that new methods can improve geothermal exploration, but that there is no single solution capable of meeting all needs. Innovative methods are particularly useful when they complement more traditional approaches, thereby providing a more robust representation of the subsurface. Similarly, artificial intelligence offers new possibilities for analyzing large amounts of data, but it does not replace the human expertise needed to interpret the results and build a reliable picture of the subsurface. Storing Heat UndergroundThe second section focused on thermal storage underground and its potential to bring greater flexibility to the energy system. The SFOE’s strategic and regulatory perspective was supplemented by several case studies from pilot projects, such as thermal storage in a Quaternary aquifer at theZurich Airport and the project aimed at seasonally storing waste heat underground at the Forsthaus (BE) power plant, which notably allowed for the exploration of various approaches to increase the reservoir’s transmissivity. Practical insights into the environmental monitoring of groundwater in a high-temperature storage system within a geothermal well field on the Empa-Eawag campus were also presented. Finally, the aquifer temperature observatory in Sion provided an opportunity to discuss methods for characterizing and monitoring the thermal evolution of an aquifer on a regional scale, as well as practical aspects related to measuring the effects of thermal groundwater extraction. All of this feedback, particularly regarding environmental monitoring and surveillance, provides an essential foundation for developing the framework conditions necessary for the effective deployment of these storage systems in Switzerland. Next-Generation Geothermal SystemsIn the final part of the workshop, an overview was provided of several approaches to developing next-generation geothermal systems (next-gen technologies). Notably presented were modular closed-loop AGS (Advanced Geothermal Systems) using technology developed by EAPOSYS, as well as the AgenS project in the Upper Rhine Graben, which relies on the development of multilateral wells from a single vertical borehole to reduce seismic risk. Reducing seismic risk is also at the heart of innovative work related to EGS (Enhanced Geothermal System) technology, as illustrated by the Haute-Sorne (JU), as well as the research conducted by the InEarth project to better understand seismicity induced by fluid injections during hydraulic stimulation. Finally, discussions focused on new approaches to heat storage in fractured rocks and low-permeability reservoirs, particularly in crystalline rocks. These concepts rely on hydraulic stimulation techniques similar to those used for EGS systems. An Essential CollaborationThe discussions showed that the subsurface can play an important role in the energy transition, whether for producing or storing energy. To achieve this, reliable subsurface characterization and innovative technologies are required. To harness this potential in a safe, sustainable, and economically viable manner, close collaboration between research, industry, and government remains essential. Sharing data and knowledge will also be a key factor for success.

items.title: SHAM-Bench: A Span-level Hallucination Benchmark Across Multiple Tasks
items.abstract: Span-level hallucination detection pinpoints unsupported content in LLM outputs, enabling actionable feedback and targeted mitigation. Existing evaluations for span-level hallucination detection methods are fragmented across tasks, annotation formats, and metrics, and most span-level datasets cover only a single NLG domain, making it difficult to assess whether a detection method actually generalizes across tasks and domains. In this paper, we introduce SHAM-Bench (Span-level Hallucination Benchmark Across Multiple Tasks), a unified benchmark for span-level hallucination detection spanning six NLG tasks, aggregated from existing human-annotated datasets totaling 6,461 examples under a common schema and evaluation protocol. Using SHAM-Bench, we evaluate existing hallucination detection methods and find that fine-tuned detectors often perform well in-domain but degrade under distribution shift, whereas prompt-based methods with reasoning are more robust across tasks. Our analysis further shows that subtle unsupported content remains difficult to detect and span-level evaluation is still challenged by ambiguous span boundaries and noisy labels. We release the dataset, evaluation code, and a public leaderboard to support future research on broadly generalizable hallucination detection.

items.title: Shaped SAEs: Expanding the Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability
items.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) seek to decompose the dense activations of large language models (LLMs) into sparse, potentially interpretable features using a learned overcomplete dictionary. In this work, we ask whether it is possible to enhance the semantic selectivity of the learned dictionary atoms by linearly \emph{shaping} the dense activations prior to learning an SAE. We explore rank-reducing transformations based on the recently introduced J-space corresponding to the averaged Jacobian from the current layer to the LLM output, projecting activations onto the ``live'' subspace spanned by eigenmodes of the Jacobian with larger singular values (which we expect to be more semantically relevant). We also introduce a new approach for training SAEs in which (a)~an affine shaping transformation is learned along with the dictionary atoms, (b)~the atom selection mechanism is based on the TopK projections along the one-dimensional subspace spanned by the atoms, and (c)~reconstruction is carried out using the same atoms. We call this approach a Matched Filter SAE (MF-SAE) based on analogies with communication theory. The promise of shaping is demonstrated via evaluations against dense activations and state-of-the-art SAEs on benchmarks including SAEBench and SAE Probes.

items.title: Shariah Liability for Artificial Intelligence Errors in Concluding Islamic Financial Contracts
items.abstract: This study examines a contemporary fiqh issue concerning the determination of Shariah liability for artificial intelligence errors in the conclusion of Islamic financial contracts within the banking and financial sectors. The research problem lies in the absence of a conclusive fiqh characterization of the nature of the role played by artificial intelligence technologies in contractual processes: whether they should be regarded merely as rigid technical tools for execution, or whether their autonomous actions may be analogically characterized in light of the rules of wakālah (agency) and niyābah (representation), and the implications of such characterization for determining the party responsible for ḍamān when technical errors or unauthorized actions occur. The study adopts inductive, analytical, and comparative approaches by examining the fiqh rules governing contracts, ḍamān, causation, and tafrīṭ (negligence), and comparing them with contemporary technological functions. The study concludes, among other findings, that artificial intelligence does not possess independent Shariah legal capacity or a separate financial liability, and that its actions remain governed by the nature of the authorities granted to it and the human inputs involved. It further establishes that the machine cannot be attributed independent fiqh reasoning. The study also concludes that Shariah liability and the rules of ḍamān may be distributed among the programming entity, the financial institution using the system, and the human supervisor, according to the relevant criteria of negligence, tafrīṭ, or errors in system design and data. The study recommends the development of regulatory frameworks and robust Shariah guidelines, together with strengthening qualified human oversight to ensure the integrity of financial transactions and compliance with Shariah requirements.

items.title: Sim-to-Real Transfer Through Adaptive Post-Training for Autonomous Driving in Unseen Environments
items.abstract: Autonomous driving systems increasingly depend on simulation for scalable training, yet the transfer of learned policies to unseen real-world environments remains a central obstacle. This paper examines sim-to-real transfer through the lens of adaptive post-training, understood not merely as a final fine-tuning step but as a socio-technical capability embedded in the lifecycle of autonomous vehicle deployment. The argument is that unseen environments expose structural limits in simulation-based development because they combine perceptual novelty, behavioral ambiguity, infrastructure irregularity, and governance uncertainty. Adaptive post-training can narrow these gaps by recalibrating representations, control policies, and safety constraints after initial training, using limited field data, targeted simulations, and operational feedback. However, such adaptation also introduces new system-level trade-offs involving architectural complexity, verification burden, data governance, fairness, sustainability, and accountability. The paper develops a conceptual framework for analyzing these trade-offs and connects them to practical concerns in autonomous driving, including operational design domains, edge-case exposure, model auditing, and infrastructure dependence. It also compares autonomous driving with robotics, aviation, and large-scale machine learning systems to clarify how post-training changes reliability engineering and policy expectations. The conclusion is that adaptive post-training is necessary but insufficient by itself; it must be paired with transparent validation, continuous monitoring, and institutional mechanisms that distribute responsibility across manufacturers, operators, regulators, and affected communities. The paper contributes a system-level research agenda for making sim-to-real transfer robust, equitable, and sustainable in unseen environments.

items.title: Síndrome de Burnout em profissionais da saúde atuantes na unidade de terapia intensiva.
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is an occupational health concern among professionals working in Intensive Care Units (ICUs), settings characterized by complex care and high physical and emotional demands. This study aimed to analyze the impacts of burnout on these professionals and its relationship with patient safety and quality of care. An integrative literature review was conducted using a qualitative, descriptive, and exploratory approach, with searches in SciELO, PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, and Google Scholar. Eligible articles were published between 2015 and 2025, available in full text, written in Portuguese, English, or Spanish, and related to the study topic. The analysis identified workload overload, long working hours, staff shortages, frequent exposure to suffering, and insufficient institutional support as factors associated with burnout. Occupational exhaustion was associated with impaired attention, communication, and decision-making, with implications for quality of care and patient safety. Prevention strategies included adequate staffing, psychological support, professional recognition, and improved working conditions. It was concluded that early recognition of burnout and the adoption of institutional prevention measures are essential to promoting professionals’ mental health and ensuring safe, humanized care in intensive care settings.

items.title: Sionna Bench: Towards Benchmarks in Wireless Communications
items.abstract: Academic research in wireless communications has no tradition of benchmarks so far. Remarkable progress in benchmark-oriented fields like machine learning suggests that the adoption of benchmarks could benefit our field. In the absence of benchmarks, however, a scientific debt has accumulated: since the academic community has not canonized specific problem setups, methods that address essentially the same problem were often developed for slightly different setups and lack a common framework for comparison. Any attempt to establish a new benchmark is faced with the challenge of resolving this debt. Recent advances in agentic artificial intelligence (AI) create an opportunity to do so by leveraging AI-assisted coding. This makes it possible to implement the state-of-the art at scale and to adapt it to a common framework for comparison. We present Sionna Bench to initiate benchmarks in academic wireless communications research. As a pilot study, we use the problem of MIMO-OFDM channel estimation. At the time of writing, Sionna Bench's channel estimation benchmark features twenty channel estimation methods that were implemented from ten different papers. The ability to compare methods against the state-of-the-art will be crucial for navigating the research landscape in an era where AI-generated methods coexist with human-developed algorithms.

items.title: Six domains in pancreatic cancer care
items.abstract: Abstract Pancreatic cancer is an aggressive malignancy with a poor prognosis and complex supportive-care needs. Individualized tumor-directed treatment remains the central axis of care, while evolving nutritional and metabolic status, biliary complications, pain, inflammatory burden, thrombotic risk, and psychological distress may affect treatment readiness, tolerance, continuity, and quality of life. This review proposes the Six-Domain Supportive Care Framework, which organizes 6 clinically relevant and interacting priorities longitudinally around individualized tumor-directed treatment: Cancer Cachexia and Metabolic Derangement, Obstructive Jaundice and Infection Risk, Perineural Invasion and Neuropathic Pain, Chronic Cholangitis and Inflammatory Burden, Cancer-Associated Thrombosis and Coagulopathy, and Psychological Distress and quality of life. We focus on pancreatic cancer-specific evidence across these domains and draw on relevant gastrointestinal and broader oncology studies when direct evidence is limited. The 6 domains also involve longitudinal information from clinical records, laboratory tests, imaging, and patient-reported outcomes. Advances in digital health and artificial intelligence (AI) create new opportunities to integrate these heterogeneous data for risk identification, longitudinal monitoring, clinical prioritization, and clinician-supervised decision support. By linking current clinical evidence with AI-assisted data integration and decision support, this framework provides a clinically oriented perspective on coordinated longitudinal supportive care in pancreatic cancer and highlights priorities for future validation and clinical translation.

items.title: SkillMatch: An Integrated Platform for AI Resume Analysis, Job Description Matching, and Interview Preparation
items.abstract: SkillMatch is a full-stack, AI-powered web application that unifies resume analysis, resume enhancement, job-description matching, cover-letter generation, and interview preparation in a single platform. It is designed to help students and job seekers understand exactly why their resumes may be rejected by Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) and what they can do to improve them. The work addresses several gaps in existing tools: most candidates do not know why their resume fails at the ATS screening stage; existing tools either give an opaque score with no explanation or solve only one part of the problem, such as a resume builder or a job board; interview preparation is typically disconnected from the candidate's actual resume content; and premium tools that offer detailed feedback are expensive and inaccessible to students. The system combines a React frontend, a Node.js/Express backend, and a PostgreSQL database, using deterministic processing for parsing, grading, and score tallying, and generative AI for rubric-based scoring, skill-gap detection, and interview-question generation. The cover-letter module saves job seekers from writer's block by automatically turning their resume and job-match data into a customized, ready-to-send pitch. The implemented platform completes the main workflow from resume submission to analysis, feedback, and career-preparation support, although AI-based scores vary slightly between runs and scanned resumes are not yet supported. Further testing with larger numbers of users and resumes is required to evaluate accuracy and effectiveness. Keywords— Applicant Tracking System; Resume Analysis; Job Description Matching; Interview Preparation; Generative AI; Cover Letter Generation

items.title: Smart questioning, answering, and clarifying to support adaptive learning
items.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education; however, many AI-based systems function primarily as reactive answer generators rather than adaptive instructional supports. This study develops and evaluates smart questioning, answering, and clarifying (SmartQAC), a pedagogically grounded AI-supported learning system that operationalizes structured dialogic scaffolding through questioning, answering, and clarification mechanisms to support adaptive learning. Design/methodology/approach SmartQAC integrates retrieval-augmented generation, prompt-routing strategies, and structured dialogic interactions to promote metacognitive engagement and conceptual development. A quasi-experimental study involving 52 undergraduate students was conducted within a database course as an illustrative domain application. Mixed-method analyses were performed using pre-test and post-test assessments, interaction logs, questionnaires, and interviews to examine learning achievement, learning behaviors, and learner perceptions. Findings Results indicate that students using SmartQAC achieved significantly higher learning achievement than those in the control group. Interaction behaviors within the SmartQAC environment were positively associated with students' learning achievement. Furthermore, participants reported positive perceptions regarding instructional usefulness, autonomy support, engagement, and pedagogical value. Originality/value This study demonstrates how dialogic instructional principles can be operationalized within a retrieval-augmented large language model system to support adaptive learning. The findings provide empirical evidence for the effectiveness of integrating questioning, answering, and clarification mechanisms into AI-supported learning environments and offer practical design implications for future adaptive educational systems.

items.title: Smart Skill Hub: An AI-Driven Platform for Personalized Learning, Career Tracking, And Skill Development
items.abstract: The rapid growth of software technologies has created a significant challenge for students and early-career developers: acquiring technical skills is no longer sufficient without continuously identifying skill gaps, following structured learning paths, demonstrating practical coding ability, maintaining a professional portfolio, and preparing effective resumes. Existing learning platforms generally address individual aspects of this process, resulting in fragmented workflows in which learners use multiple applications for learning, coding practice, resume creation, GitHub analysis, portfolio development, and career guidance. This paper presents Smart Skill Hub (SSH), an integrated AI-powered skill development and career readiness platform designed to unify these activities within a single ecosystem. Smart Skill Hub combines personalized skill profiling, skill-gap analysis, AI-generated learning roadmaps, educational video discovery, coding assessment, GitHub intelligence, AI-assisted resume analysis and generation, portfolio management, analytics, and an AI-based Smart Mentor. The platform uses a modern web architecture consisting of a React and TypeScript frontend, Node.js and Express backend services, MongoDB for persistent data storage, Firebase Authentication for identity management, and centralized Large Language Model services for intelligent features. A secure Docker-based coding execution environment is used to execute programming submissions with resource and network restrictions. The platform maintains a canonical representation of learner skills and profile information so that information can be reused consistently across learning, assessment, resume, portfolio, and mentoring workflows. Resume processing supports document extraction, structured profile generation, interactive A4 editing, multiple ATS-oriented templates, AI-assisted improvement, job-specific analysis, and selectable-text PDF generation. GitHub Intelligence analyses authenticated GitHub activity to derive development insights, while analytics provide learners and administrators with measurable information about activity and system usage. Smart Skill Hub demonstrates an integrated approach to student skill development by connecting learning, assessment, professional representation, and AI-based guidance in a unified platform. The resulting system is designed to reduce fragmentation, improve personalization, and provide students with a continuous workflow from identifying skills and gaps to developing, demonstrating, and presenting those skills.

items.title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
items.abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to $π_{0.5}$, SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a $1.98\times$ full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.

items.title: Sparse RL Relaxation for LLM Reasoning
items.abstract: Recent work has explored continuous representations in place of discrete tokens during Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, often referred to as soft CoT. This is motivated by the idea that a mixture of token embeddings can represent a superposition of multiple reasoning possibilities within a single step. However, it remains challenging to train large language models to realize this potential. Existing work has explored reinforcement learning (RL)-style training for soft CoT. However, these approaches treat soft tokens as actions in a Markov decision process rather than as differentiable intermediate computation steps. Thus, they do not propagate gradients across the soft tokens and miss out on the signal of how the choice of one soft token affects the next. In this paper, we propose a sparse relaxation method for RL (called SpaRLax), which leverages the differentiability of soft-CoT reasoning over time steps and makes training more stable and effective. We adopt an entmax sparsity method that adaptively determines the degree of softness, which truncates long-tail noise at confident steps while retaining multiple plausible candidates when uncertain. Across nine reasoning benchmarks, our method achieves the highest average performance compared with baseline methods. Further analyses validate the effective use of soft-token superposition in our approach, and also demonstrate the contribution of adaptive sparsity in our approach.

items.title: Speech LLMs That Breathe: Modeling Non-Verbal Vocalizations in Dialogue
items.abstract: The user experience of speech interaction models has improved, benefiting from the modeling of paralinguistic attributes and advances in speech reconstruction paradigms. However, human communication follows extensive norms regarding non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) spanning respiratory, affective, and discourse. The omission of these events imposes inherent limitations on the naturalness of current approaches. In this work, we cover 13 major types of NVVs and construct a natural dialogue dataset that conforms to human conversational norms through an automated synthesis pipeline. We enhance the ability of speech interaction models to generate contextually appropriate NVV events through multi-stage fine-tuning and NVV-aware GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Based on distinct modeling paradigms, we substantially improve the expressiveness of VocalNet and VITA-Qinyu in empathy interactions and role-play dialogues, and further discuss the architectural necessity for achieving high-quality natural speech generation.

items.title: SPINAL-CORD Model: Integrating Human and System Factors in Modern Aviation Safety
items.abstract: Classical human factors models transformed aviation safety by shifting attention from individual blame to systemic understanding. Yet the operational landscape of modern aviation has evolved considerably: automation is pervasive, cognitive demands are higher, and understanding of neurocognition and behavioral variability is richer than when foundational frameworks were built. This paper introduces the SPINAL-CORD model, an original safety integration heuristic designed to complement, not replace, established frameworks. The model comprises two interacting components: SPINAL (Skills, Personal Factors, Intelligence, Neurocognition, Adaptability and Resilience, Learning), representing the human behavioral and cognitive core, and CORD (Computing, Organization, Rules, Data), representing the structured operational environment. Together they conceptualise safety as continuously co-produced at the human-system interface, rather than residing in either the operator or the system alone. The paper describes the model's theoretical foundations in cognitive science, resilience engineering, and systems thinking; its relationship to other models; and its practical applications in training, debriefing, and incident analysis. Limitations and directions for future empirical validation are discussed. The model offers practitioners a visual and conceptual anchor for conversations about performance, strain, and adaptive capacity in complex aviation environments.

items.title: SplatXR: A Toolkit for Multi-Layered Extended Reality via On-Headset 3D Gaussian Splatting
items.abstract: Recent advances in Gaussian splatting, 3D foundation models, and video-passthrough mixed reality offer unprecedented fidelity for capturing and blending physical and virtual worlds. However, established XR methods rely on polygon-based pipelines that treat physical and digital environments as separate domains, making seamless integration across recent novel representations difficult. Because splats lack explicit surface geometry, they impede standard graphics techniques necessary for cross-reality interactions, such as shadow or collision handling. Furthermore, while 3D foundation models can reconstruct physical objects on-the-fly into digital splats, current XR systems fall short of leveraging this capability for user experiences that transition seamlessly between physicality and virtuality. To address this, we organize XR as a multi-layered reality of interacting primitives, letting pixels and objects move across physical and digital boundaries. We contribute SplatXR, a Unity toolkit that operationalizes this structure as building blocks for interactive, immersive apps leveraging 3D Gaussian splatting: a standalone renderer, splat-to-mesh reconstruction, splat physics, splat blending, and offloaded splat object reconstruction via on-headset capture. SplatXR unites vision and graphics techniques to make splat-based XR development broadly available, and we validate it through demonstrative applications and a small developer study.

items.title: Standing on the Shoulders of Giants: Enhancing LLM Agents for Automated Fact-Checking with Human Expert Skills
items.abstract: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems powered by large language model (LLM) agents still face challenges in evidence retrieval and claim verification. Existing approaches improve their capabilities through computationally costly post-training or human-in-the-loop feedback that is difficult to scale. To transfer professional fact-checking expertise to LLM agents efficiently, we distill publicly available guidelines published by Agence France-Presse (AFP) Fact Check into a reusable, modular Professional Fact-Checking Skill (PFC-Skill). We then present SkillCheck, the first AFC system that gives LLM agents dynamic access to PFC-Skill to guide evidence retrieval and claim verification at inference time. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SkillCheck improves upon skill-free DEFAME baselines across multiple LLM backbones, with gains of 2.2--4.8 pp. in Accuracy and 1.5--6.3 pp. in Macro-F1 on the AVeriTeC benchmark. Notably, SkillCheck with GPT-4o-Mini exceeds DEFAME with GPT-4o by 3.4 pp. in Accuracy while cutting inference cost by roughly 61%. The performance gains also extend to open-web retrieval. Ablations show that incorporating the skill during evidence retrieval provides most of the gains, while incorporation into both stages yields the best overall performance. Case studies show that PFC-Skill enables more targeted search and closer scrutiny of evidence. To conclude, our work shows that LLM agents can "stand on the shoulders of giants" by drawing on the best practices of professional fact-checkers, substantially enhancing AFC performance without extra training or continuous human supervision.

items.title: Steering an LLM AutoResearch Loop with Domain Context: A Case Study with Vehicle Energy Models
items.abstract: Research Software Engineers (RSEs) often work with Machine Learning (ML) models integratedinto scientific software stacks, and incremental model improvements are valuable but expensivein human time and attention. Our team maintains RouteE-Powertrain, which predicts vehicleenergy consumption and is integrated into RouteE-Compass for energy-aware routing.We investigated whether a Large Language Model (LLM) agent could help accelerate thediscovery process for model improvements by taking on certain elements that are challengingfor us, like context switching and managing limited time budgets. We began with an existingautomated research harness (Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch) where an agent canrepeatedly modify the model and then evaluate against a held-out dataset. This harness foundlarge improvements in our error metrics, but upon further inspection, the winning model wasunusable in our application domain. Specifically, it used unobservable future road network linkstates that are not compatible with our energy-aware route planning application and yielded avery large compute cost at inference time, leading to prohibitive computational overhead forroute planning. We also identified the need for additional agent instruction around logging,single-variable experimentation, token accounting, and trial budgets to support improvedanalysis. We accumulated these discoveries into a modified harness that would guide the agentwithin our narrower optimization space.We then ran two sessions over the same modified harness, each ~50 trials, ~8 hours wall time,~$35 token cost. The first session included our complete modified harness, whereas the secondsession excluded only the domain-specific guidance. Both sessions were then audited in anenvironment where only valid input features were used, for one million model evaluations. Theunguided experiment chose a final model of an ensemble of 75% GBDT/25% CNN and reporteda better overall RMSE score, but when audited, the model performed even worse than thebaseline and took 951 seconds to run one million evaluations (0.95ms/eval). The domain-guidedexperiment produced a 2x128 MLP with a properly constrained feature set which reduced ournetwork link-level RMSE by 49% and completed the audit in 1.4 seconds (0.0014ms/eval).Grounding the agent with explicit deployment constraints ensured that all improvementsremained usable in our application, highlighting that human-in-the-loop domain context is criticalfor this type of automated discovery.We have open sourced the modified harness, along with the archive of the two experimentsessions, with the hope that this will be a valuable resource for other RSE teams whomaintain ML models.
